listenings.text: At twenty-one, I was ranked in the top two hundred in the world, and I really believed I could go further. Then, when I was twenty-two, I hurt my shoulder in a match in Barcelona. Two operations later, my career as a player was over. For a long time, I asked myself the same question. What would have happened if I hadn't been injured? Honestly, I think I would have played for a few more years, but I probably wouldn't have become a top player. My serve was never strong enough. Now I coach young players at a club in Manchester, and I love it. If I hadn't stopped so early, I would never have discovered how much I enjoy teaching.

For twenty years, I worked in a bank in Lyon. It was a good job, with a good salary, and very safe. But I wasn't happy. When I was forty-five, I left the bank and started a small company that makes parts for bicycles. My wife supported me from the first day, but my parents thought I was crazy. The first two years were very hard, and I almost gave up twice. Today we have forty employees, and we sell to twelve countries. People sometimes ask me what my life would be like if I hadn't taken the risk. The answer is simple. I would probably still be working in the same bank, in the same office, and I would still be asking myself, what if?

Twelve years ago, I was a young engineer in Chennai, and one evening I received an email from a Japanese company. They were opening a new plant and they wanted engineers from India. I almost deleted it. I thought it was spam. My friend told me to read it again, and I did. Two months later, I was in Nagoya, and I didn't speak a word of Japanese. People ask me if I have regrets about leaving my family and my country. I don't. If I hadn't gone, I would never have learned Japanese, and I wouldn't have met my wife, who was my teacher. And if I had deleted that email, I would be a very different person today.

paras: When I was nineteen, tennis was my whole life. I trained every morning before school, and I played tournaments every weekend. That year, after I won the state championship, a university in Florida offered me a scholarship. It was the dream of every young player in Brazil: four years of studies, coaching and college tennis in America.

But that same month, my father became sick, and a factory near our house offered me a job as a trainee. I was at a crossroads. If I went to Florida, my mother would be alone with my father and my two little sisters. So I turned down the scholarship, and I took the job. For a few years, I didn't touch a racket. I didn't want to think about what I had lost.

Forty years later, I am the director of that company. I sometimes ask myself what would have happened if I had accepted the scholarship. I would have played in America, and I might have become a coach. But if I hadn't taken that job, I wouldn't have met my wife, who worked in the same office, and I wouldn't be where I am today. In hindsight, the factory was my turning point. Today my wife and I play doubles every Saturday, and my only regret is my serve.
